title: Nine in Ten Indian Adults Have Abnormal Cholesterol, Landmark ICMR Study Finds
excerpt: The ICMR-INDIAB study of 23,665 adults reveals 87.3% have at least one lipid abnormality, with an estimated 355 million affected even without diabetes, obesity, or hypertension.
body:
• The ICMR-INDIAB study found 87.3% of Indian adults have at least one abnormal lipid level, with low HDL cholesterol the most common issue affecting nearly two-thirds of the population.
  • An estimated 355 million Indians have dyslipidemia despite having normal blood sugar, blood pressure, and body weight — challenging the practice of testing cholesterol only in those with existing conditions.
  • Risk peaks between ages 30 and 39, a decade earlier than many clinicians screen, and women are more affected than men.
  • South Asian ancestry is classified as a "risk-enhancing factor" in the 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guidelines, meaning diaspora Indians should discuss early lipid screening with their doctors.

Nearly nine out of every ten Indian adults carry at least one abnormal lipid marker in their blood, according to the largest nationwide lipid survey ever conducted in India.

The ICMR-INDIAB study, led by the Indian Council of Medical Research, analysed lipid profiles of 23,665 adults drawn from every state and Union Territory. It found that 87.3 per cent had dyslipidemia — an unhealthy balance of fats in the blood that is a leading driver of heart attacks and strokes.

Low HDL dominates the picture

The most common abnormality was low high-density lipoprotein (HDL), or "good" cholesterol, which affected roughly two-thirds of all adults tested. Elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high triglycerides, and raised total cholesterol were also widespread.

What makes the findings particularly alarming is the scale among seemingly healthy people. Researchers estimated that around 355 million Indians have abnormal lipid levels despite having normal blood sugar, normal blood pressure, and no obesity. The data challenge a common clinical assumption that cholesterol testing is only necessary for patients who already have diabetes or hypertension.

"Indians are genetically predisposed to low HDL cholesterol, but lifestyle factors play an equally important role. Carbohydrate-heavy diets increase triglyceride levels and reduce HDL cholesterol."

— Dr V. Mohan, Chairman, Dr Mohan's Diabetes Specialities Centre and study co-author

The Asian Indian Phenotype

Clinicians have long described a metabolic pattern common among South Asians sometimes called the "Asian Indian Phenotype" — characterised by higher abdominal fat, insulin resistance, low HDL, and elevated triglycerides even at a normal body mass index. The ICMR data confirm that this pattern is not confined to urban elites or older age groups. Dyslipidemia peaked in the 30-to-39 age bracket, suggesting cardiovascular risk accumulates far earlier than many people realise.

Women had a higher prevalence than men, while urban residents were more affected than rural populations, though the urban-rural gap was relatively narrow. The findings underscore that lipid disorders cut across geography, income, and gender in India.

Treatment gap compounds the risk

Even among those who know they have heart disease, lipid control remains inadequate. A separate nationwide survey published in JACC: Asia examined 9,658 Indian patients with documented coronary artery disease who were on stable lipid-lowering therapy. Despite 73 per cent receiving high-intensity statins, only 27 per cent achieved the recommended LDL-C target of 50 mg/dL or below. Combination therapies that could close the gap — such as adding ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors to statins — were used in just 12 per cent of cases.

The authors described the shortfall as a product of "clinician inertia," noting that treating doctors adjusted the regimen in only 37 per cent of patients whose LDL remained above target.

Why it matters for the diaspora

The cardiovascular implications extend well beyond India's borders. The 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol management guidelines formally classified South Asian ancestry as a "risk-enhancing factor" — one of only a handful of ethnic designations singled out. The designation means that Indian Americans and other South Asian diaspora populations should be considered for earlier and more aggressive lipid screening, even when standard risk calculators show moderate scores.

Research from the MASALA study, a longitudinal cohort of South Asian Americans in San Francisco and Chicago, has shown that South Asians in the United States have significantly lower HDL levels, higher triglycerides, and more small dense LDL particles compared with white counterparts. Diabetes prevalence runs at roughly 25 per cent — more than double the national average — often appearing at a lower BMI and a younger age.

"The risk estimators used in clinical practice have important limitations when it comes to diverse patient populations. Zero South Asians were included in the cohort studies used to develop them."

— Dr Amit Khera, Cardiologist, UT Southwestern Medical Center

Diet and next steps

Dr Mohan recommended what he calls the "plate concept" as a practical dietary framework: one-quarter of the plate should be carbohydrates, one-quarter protein, and the remaining half vegetables and fruits. The advice targets the traditional Indian diet, where refined carbohydrates from white rice or wheat flour can constitute 60 to 70 per cent of daily calories, directly driving up triglycerides and suppressing HDL.

The study's authors have called for universal lipid screening of all adults beginning at age 20, rather than limiting testing to those already diagnosed with metabolic conditions. With cardiovascular disease now the leading cause of death in India — responsible for more than a quarter of all deaths — the case for early, population-wide intervention has never been stronger.
